proposedActions: Propose a six-week pilot comparing fixed-threshold rules with site-specific statistical/one-class baselines on both protocols, without attack-labelled training or calibration. Use separate chronological training, tuning and evaluation samples; check temporal independence and include unseen sites calibrated only on their earlier traffic. Randomly sample all evaluation windows, with and without alerts, for expert labelling; count uncertain cases separately. Evaluate detection only on controlled bench injections or confirmed cases. Measure labelled-window false-positive rate, false alerts/site/day, scenario recall, detection delay, explanation comprehension, CPU, RAM and forwarding latency. Negotiable go/no-go targets for the best configuration, whichever it is: at most one false alert/site/day, at least 80% injected-scenario detection within 60 seconds for each protocol, and 80% correct explanation interpretation by plant managers. Require attack-free training/calibration, authorised access, Yocto on-device execution within agreed budgets, and no measurable forwarding-latency increase under agreed representative loads. Treat insufficient labels or unmet gates as reasons to revise or stop, not evidence of success.

During proposed weeks one and two, company engineers could inventory permitted captures, operating regimes and appliance limits, arrange expert review, and define representative BACnet services and safe bench scenarios. Kiss could propose features, split checks and evaluation procedures. Execute the NDA and data-sharing agreement before transferring data or using the university testbed.

During proposed weeks three through six, Kiss could lead baseline comparison and BACnet transfer testing while company engineers implement profiling and alert templates. Include maintenance and configuration changes, test operator-authorised baseline resets, and document missed scenarios and uncertain labels. Review results against the first experiment's gates before considering field integration.

content.markdown:
# Site-specific, explainable anomaly detection for ProtoSense

## Verified facts
- ArmaturaSec reports no malicious traffic examples and acknowledges that clients could have been compromised unknowingly. Training and operational calibration therefore need to work without confirmed attacks; the archives must be treated as unlabelled, not guaranteed clean. [F1]
- The company needs site-specific detection for both Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP. Its previous classifier generated deployment false positives that led clients to disable alerts; explanations must be understandable to a plant manager. [F2]
- ArmaturaSec says it has hardware for on-device inference and uses custom Yocto Linux. Its hardware plan targets anomaly detection without affecting packet-forwarding latency; this does not establish current processor availability or numerical resource budgets. [F3]
- The company offers one to two part-time engineers and archive, bench and firmware access under NDA. Kiss's group makes its testbed available under a data-sharing agreement. [F4]
- Kiss's Modbus research constructs per-register baselines using request intervals, payload values and function-code sequences, providing a concrete starting method. [F5]
- Her incremental-model study found that legitimate process reconfiguration produced a persistent anomaly episode and tested an operator-acknowledged reset. This identifies an adaptation risk relevant to nuisance alerts. [F6]
- Kiss lists openness to joint projects with ICS monitoring companies; this is general willingness, not a commitment to this project. [F7]

## Potential benefits
- For the company: The pilot could show whether either tested configuration reduces nuisance alerts while retaining useful, understandable detection on both protocols within actual appliance limits.
- For the researcher: Subject to agreement and permissions, Kiss could test how statistical baselines transfer to BACnet and changing operational sites, using client captures, reviewed windows and controlled bench scenarios.

## Our inference
- Site-specific statistical baselines could offer a more understandable starting point than transferring a public-dataset classifier. Timing, value and command deviations could support explanations, but explanation usefulness still needs testing.
- The supplied evidence does not establish BACnet performance or fit on ArmaturaSec appliances. Protocol transfer, unseen-site calibration and device profiling are separate validation gaps; injected scenarios cannot establish recall against unknown operational attacks.
- This joint-project proposal is conditional because researcher availability is unknown. Limited engineering time and unresolved permissions suggest a narrowly scoped pilot rather than an immediate production commitment.

## Proposed next steps
- Propose a six-week pilot comparing fixed-threshold rules with site-specific statistical/one-class baselines on both protocols, without attack-labelled training or calibration. Use separate chronological training, tuning and evaluation samples; check temporal independence and include unseen sites calibrated only on their earlier traffic. Randomly sample all evaluation windows, with and without alerts, for expert labelling; count uncertain cases separately. Evaluate detection only on controlled bench injections or confirmed cases. Measure labelled-window false-positive rate, false alerts/site/day, scenario recall, detection delay, explanation comprehension, CPU, RAM and forwarding latency. Negotiable go/no-go targets for the best configuration, whichever it is: at most one false alert/site/day, at least 80% injected-scenario detection within 60 seconds for each protocol, and 80% correct explanation interpretation by plant managers. Require attack-free training/calibration, authorised access, Yocto on-device execution within agreed budgets, and no measurable forwarding-latency increase under agreed representative loads. Treat insufficient labels or unmet gates as reasons to revise or stop, not evidence of success.
- During proposed weeks one and two, company engineers could inventory permitted captures, operating regimes and appliance limits, arrange expert review, and define representative BACnet services and safe bench scenarios. Kiss could propose features, split checks and evaluation procedures. Execute the NDA and data-sharing agreement before transferring data or using the university testbed.
- During proposed weeks three through six, Kiss could lead baseline comparison and BACnet transfer testing while company engineers implement profiling and alert templates. Include maintenance and configuration changes, test operator-authorised baseline resets, and document missed scenarios and uncertain labels. Review results against the first experiment's gates before considering field integration.

## Open questions
- Can Kiss confirm availability and proposed effort for this joint project, and can both parties agree its start, funding, milestones and responsibilities?
- Which current appliance, traffic loads, CPU/RAM budgets and latency measurement tolerance should define acceptance?
- Can client permissions and the required agreements support capture review, representative BACnet bench tests and the proposed evaluation splits?
- Who will agree the provisional acceptance targets, label ambiguous windows, recruit plant-manager reviewers and authorise baseline updates?
